name: Week in Review
desc: Finish sentences about your week and add details.
instr: Choose three sentences and finish them about your week. Add a detail or an example to each one.
cards: A small win this week was…
I wish I'd had more time to…
The best moment of my week was…
Next week I'm looking forward to…
coverP: a weekly planner open on a desk with a coffee, a pen and sticky notes

name: Strange Delivery
desc: A mystery parcel arrives. What do you do with it?
instr: A parcel arrives at your door with no note. Choose one item. What would you do or say, and why?
ph: The first thing I'd do is…
cards: A plane ticket to a secret destination
A cake with your face on it
A letter from your future self
A suitcase full of old coins
imgP: an open cardboard parcel on a doorstep containing {x}

name: My Go-To
desc: Your favourite, always-reliable choices.
instr: Your 'go-to' is the thing you always choose. Pick three and explain them in 2–3 sentences each.
coverP: a cosy flat lay of favourite everyday things: a mug, headphones, a snack, a book and trainers

name: Main Character
desc: Today your life is a film. Describe it.
instr: Imagine today is a film and you are the main character. Answer the questions with true details.
ph: In the background you can hear…
cards: What's the title of the film?
coverP: an old cinema clapperboard and a film camera on a city street at golden hour

name: Mood Menu
desc: Order one to three 'moods' that match how you feel.
instr: This is today's mood menu. Order one to three options that match how you feel right now and say why.
ph: Right now I'm in the mood for…
cards: Stay under a blanket all day
imgP: a cosy scene that captures the mood: {x}

name: Ideal Weekend
desc: Plan your perfect weekend in detail.
instr: Imagine your perfect weekend. Answer the questions with as many details as you can.
cards: What time would you wake up?
Who would you spend it with?
What would you do on Sunday night?
coverP: a sunny Saturday morning: breakfast on a balcony with a view

name: How Often?
desc: Say how often you do everyday things and why.
instr: Read the card. How often do you do this? Say why.
imgP: an everyday scene illustrating the activity '{x}'

name: Name Three
desc: Name three things for each card, then compare.
instr: Read the card and name three things. Then compare with your classmates. Did anyone say the same?
cards: things you take to the beach
things you do before school or work
things you can buy with 5 euros
animals you can see on a farm
things you have in your pocket
imgP: a scene representing the category '{x}', showing several examples

name: I Use It For…
desc: Look at the object and say how you use it.
instr: Look at the picture. Think about your life. Say two or three sentences about how you use it.

name: Define It
desc: Write your own definition with three ideas.
instr: Create your own definition. Use three simple ideas or examples.
ex: A lazy Sunday: It's a day when you don't set an alarm. Usually, it means staying in your pyjamas. For me, it's when I watch films all afternoon.
coverP: an open dictionary on a wooden table with a magnifying glass

name: My User Manual
desc: Finish sentences from your own 'instruction manual'.
instr: Imagine you come with an instruction manual. Finish the sentence with something true about you and give an example.
cards: If you want to make me happy, …
If I go quiet, it means…
The best way to cheer me up is…
If you invite me to dinner, …
If you send me a message, …
coverP: an open instruction manual booklet next to a cup of tea

name: Five-Star Review
desc: Rate a life experience from 1 to 5 stars, like an online review.
instr: Rate this experience from 1 to 5 stars. Tell the story behind your rating: what happened, the best part, the worst part, and would you recommend it?
cards: Your first day at a new school or job
imgP: a scene representing the experience: {x}

name: Red Flag, Green Flag
desc: Share your own red and green flags in a situation.
instr: Read the situation. What's your own red flag and green flag here? Then talk about common ones people have.
ph: A green flag for me is when someone…
I have to admit I tend to…
coverP: a red flag and a green flag waving on a beach against a blue sky

name: The Great Swap
desc: Keep the first option or swap it for the second?
instr: Would you keep the first option or swap it for the second one? Give at least one reason.

cards.b: A walk in a snowy forest
Rainy nights with a blanket and a film

name: Done, Try or Skip
desc: Three activities: which have you done, which would you try, which would you skip?
instr: Look at the three activities. Which one have you done? Which would you love to try? Which would you skip?
cards: Spend a day without your phone
Visit a country where you don't speak the language
Dye your hair a crazy colour
Try a food you can't pronounce
imgP: the activity: {x}

name: Two Truths and a Lie
desc: Say three things about yourself. The others find the lie.
instr: Use the topic on the card. Say three sentences about yourself: two are true, one is a lie. The others ask up to three questions, then vote.
ph: I think number … is the lie because…
ex: Topic: food. 1) I once ate a cricket. 2) I can't stand chocolate. 3) My grandmother taught me to make paella.
end: Who was the best liar? Which lie was the hardest to spot?
coverP: a detective magnifying glass over three paper cards on a table

name: Unwritten Rules
desc: Is it OK or not OK? Talk about the rules nobody writes down.
instr: Read the situation. Is it OK or not? Is there an unwritten rule about it? Give your opinion and an example.
cards: Reclining your seat on a short flight
Leaving a group chat without saying anything
Arriving 15 minutes late to a party
Going to a dinner without bringing anything
Taking a phone call in a restaurant
Asking someone how much they earn
Sending a voice message longer than two minutes
Sitting next to a stranger on an empty bus
Watching the next episode of a series without your partner
Eating someone else's food in the office fridge
Not replying to a message for three days
imgP: an everyday scene of this situation: {x}

name: There's a Catch
desc: A dream offer… with conditions in the small print.
instr: This offer sounds like a dream! Add 3–5 conditions that make it less attractive. Would your partner still say yes?
ph: Oh, and you'll also have to…
ex: A free house by the sea… but you can never leave the town, you must paint it pink every year, and the neighbours are 30 seagulls.
cards: A free house by the sea
Unlimited free flights for a year
Your favourite singer plays at your birthday
A month off with full pay
Speaking every language in the world
A holiday on a private island
imgP: a dreamy, attractive photo of: {x}

name: The Job Nobody Wants
desc: Would you accept these small, annoying roles?
instr: Read the role. Would you accept it?
q: Would you accept this role? Why or why not?
What would be difficult about it?
ph: I'd be happy to… as long as…
cards: The friend who drives everyone home after the party
The one who tells the group the trip is cancelled
The person who collects the money for a present
The one who always carries the heaviest bag
The one who tests the water before everyone swims
The person who reads all the terms and conditions
The one who wakes everyone up on holiday
The neighbour who keeps everyone's spare keys
The one who chooses the music in the car
The person who writes the group's birthday messages
The one who orders for the whole table
The person who has to say no to the boss
imgP: a slightly funny everyday scene of: {x}

name: Designed to Hook You
desc: How do products keep us coming back?
instr: How was this designed to keep people using it? What makes it attractive, fun or hard to stop?
ph: What makes it so effective is…
ex: Streaks in a language app: missing a day feels like losing something you've built, so you open the app even when you're tired.
cards: New clothes in shops every week
imgP: a photo representing: {x} (generic, no real brands or app logos)

name: Convenient or Creepy?
desc: Technology that helps… and watches.
instr: Is this convenient, creepy or both? What are the benefits and the privacy risks? Where would you draw the line?
ph: I can see the benefits, especially if…
I'd accept it as long as…
That's where I'd draw the line.
cards: Your fridge orders milk when it runs out
A shop recognises your face and greets you by name
Your car tells your insurance company how you drive
Your phone suggests replies that sound exactly like you
Your smartwatch alerts your doctor automatically
An app knows when you're about to cancel
A school uses cameras to check students' attention
Your smart speaker is always listening for its name
Your bank predicts you'll run out of money
Your boss can see how much you type
Your family can always see your location
Ads for something you only talked about
imgP: a photo of this technology scenario: {x}

name: Parallel Realities
desc: Find the deeper connection between two very different ideas.
instr: Look beyond the surface. What do these two ideas have in common at a deeper level?
ph: At their core, both are about…
In both cases, you have to…

name: Headline vs Real Life
desc: Does an imagined headline match your experience?
instr: Imagine you read this headline. Does it match what you see in real life?
q: Does it sound believable? Why or why not?
Does your own experience support it or challenge it?
Why might real life be different from the data?
ph: People tend to say one thing and do another.

cards.s: 7 in 10 people check their phone within 10 minutes of waking up
cards.q: Is that a problem, or just modern life?

cards.s: Most people say they would earn less to work four days a week
cards.q: Would you? What would you do with the extra day?

cards.s: 6 in 10 students say exams don't show what they really know
cards.q: What would be a fairer way to assess students?

cards.s: Most drivers think they're better than average
cards.q: Why are we so bad at judging ourselves?

cards.s: 1 in 3 adults has never cooked a full meal from scratch
cards.q: Is cooking still an essential skill?

cards.s: Most people prefer texting to phone calls
cards.q: When is a call still better?

cards.s: Half of people have bought something online they never used
cards.q: What makes us buy things we don't need?

cards.s: 4 in 10 people say they work better from home
cards.q: What do we lose when we don't share an office?

cards.s: Most people say they'd quit social media for a year if you paid them
cards.q: How much would someone have to pay you?

cards.s: Most people say they want to travel more sustainably, but flights keep growing
cards.q: Whose responsibility is it: people's or governments'?

note: These headlines are invented for discussion, not real statistics.
coverP: a pile of newspapers and a smartphone showing a chart, on a café table

name: Defend the Object
desc: Convince everyone that an ordinary object is the best invention ever.
instr: Convince everyone that this is the most important invention of all time. How has it changed people's lives?
end: Vote: which object won the debate?

name: Would You Rather
desc: Pick a side and give two reasons.
instr: Choose one option and give two reasons. Then try to defend the other one!
imgP: a photo representing: {x}

name: Speed Debate
desc: Two minutes per side on light, funny motions.
instr: Side A argues for, side B argues against. Two minutes each, then 30 seconds to reply.
cards: Breakfast is the most important meal
Everyone should learn to cook at school
It's OK to recline your seat on a plane
Board games are better than video games
end: Class vote: which debate was the most convincing?
imgP: a playful photo representing the topic: {x}

name: Just a Minute
desc: Talk for 60 seconds without hesitating or repeating.
instr: Speak for one minute about the topic. No long pauses, no repeating yourself, don't go off topic!
cards: The best smell in the world

name: Fortunately, Unfortunately
desc: Build a silly story with alternating good and bad news.
instr: Continue the story. Take turns: one sentence starts with 'Fortunately…', the next with 'Unfortunately…'.
cards: I woke up late on Monday.
I found a wallet in the street.
My best friend invited me to a party.
The plane landed in the wrong country.
My phone fell into the sea.
The teacher gave us a surprise test.
imgP: the story moment: {x}

name: Alibi
desc: Two suspects, one story. Find the differences.
instr: Two suspects plan their alibi for the time of the 'crime' outside the room (5 minutes). The detectives prepare questions. Then each suspect is questioned alone.
q: Where were you between 7 and 9 pm?
ph: Are you sure? Your partner said…
cards: Someone ate the teacher's birthday cake.
Someone painted a moustache on the head teacher's portrait.
All the classroom chairs are on the roof.
The neighbour's garden gnome has gone missing.
Someone changed every phone alarm to 4 am.
The last slice of pizza vanished from the staff room.
Someone hid the TV remote, and the final is tonight.
end: Guilty or not guilty? If their stories differ in three details, they're guilty!
imgP: a funny scene of the aftermath: {x}

name: Taboo
desc: Describe the word without the forbidden words.
instr: Projected version: one student sits with their back to the screen. Their team describes the word without saying the forbidden words. Printed version: students take a card and describe it to their team.
coverP: a stack of blank game cards and a sand timer on a table

name: Desert Island
desc: Agree on the five things to take with you.
instr: Your group is going to live on a desert island for a month. You can only take five things. Agree together in 8 minutes.
ph: I think we should take… because…
end: Each group presents its five items. Which group would survive?
imgP: {x} lying on a sandy tropical beach

name: Hot Seat
desc: Interview a student who plays a role.
instr: One student sits in the hot seat and plays the role on the card. The class asks questions for three minutes.
q: What's a normal day like for you?
What's the best and worst part?
cards: A teacher on the last day of school
A chef at a busy restaurant
A ghost in an old castle
printNote: Guessing version: give the student a secret role card. The class asks yes/no questions until someone guesses who they are.
imgP: {x}, shown through their setting, uniform or tools

name: Story Chain
desc: Tell a story together using three random words.
instr: Tell a story together. Each person adds one or two sentences and must use one of the words, with a linker.

name: Fake Definitions
desc: A real but very strange English word. Invent a convincing definition and fool the others.
instr: This is a real English word. Invent a definition that sounds true. Then everyone votes for the one they believe. The next slide shows the real meaning.
ph: For example: 'My uncle is a real…'
I'm sure it means… because it sounds like…

cards.ans: a fuss or commotion, usually about something unimportant
in the opposite direction to the sun; anticlockwise
a nervous feeling in your stomach
to waste time doing nothing useful
the pleasant smell of rain on dry ground
a silly person who talks too much
to leave or run away very quickly
crooked, not in a straight line
small bits and pieces, or gadgets you don't know the name of
a clever but dishonest person, especially a politician
to leave suddenly without saying goodbye

ind: Show the word. You and the student each invent a definition and say an example sentence.
Mix in the real definition (don't show the next slide yet) and let the student guess which is real.
Reveal and compare. Swap roles: the student reads three definitions to you.
pair: Show the word. Each pair writes one fake definition and one example sentence.
Pairs read their definition to another pair, who guess if it's real.
Reveal the real meaning on the next slide.
grp: Show the word. Teams of 3 write a convincing fake definition in 2 minutes.
Collect them, add the real one (read it from the next slide without showing it) and read all aloud.
Everyone votes. A team scores 1 point for each vote its fake gets, and 2 points for guessing the real one. Then reveal.

end: Which fake definition was the most convincing today?

name: Sell It To Me
desc: Combine two random things into a product and pitch it to a very specific customer.
instr: Combine the two things into one product, then sell it to this customer. You have one minute to convince them!
ph: It's perfect for someone like you because…

cards.t: Customer: a grandmother who loves gardening
Customer: a teenager who never wakes up on time

ind: Show the card. Give the student one minute to prepare and one minute to pitch.
You play the customer: ask difficult questions and raise objections.
Swap roles on the next card.
pair: One student is the seller, the other is the customer, who must play the role on the card.
Seller pitches for one minute, then the customer asks two questions and decides: buy or not?
Swap roles.
grp: In teams, students get two minutes to invent the product and its name.
One person per team pitches to the class, who play the customer.
Class votes for the product they'd actually buy.

end: Which product would actually sell? What would you call it?

name: Excuses, Excuses
desc: Invent the most creative excuse for an awkward situation.
instr: You're in trouble! Invent the most creative (but believable) excuse. Then the others decide if they believe you.
cards: You arrive 40 minutes late to your best friend's birthday dinner.
You forgot to do your homework, again.
You ate your flatmate's birthday cake.
Your teacher sees you on social media when you said you were ill.
You lost the keys to a friend's car.
You fell asleep in an important meeting.
Your dog is in the swimming pool of the hotel.
You broke your neighbour's window with a ball.
You sent a message about your boss… to your boss.
You missed your own surprise party.
You're wearing two different shoes at an interview.

ind: Show the situation. The student gives an excuse; you react as the angry person and ask questions.
Push for details until the story falls apart (or doesn't!).
Swap: you give an excuse and the student judges it.
pair: Student A is in trouble, Student B is the angry person. A has 30 seconds to explain.
B asks three follow-up questions, then decides: forgive or not?
Swap roles on the next card.
grp: Show the situation and give everyone 30 seconds to think.
Pick three students to give their excuse.
The class votes: most creative and most believable.

end: Who gave the best excuse today?

name: Hot Takes
desc: Controversial (but harmless) opinions. Agree, disagree and defend your position.
instr: Here's a hot take. Do you agree or disagree? Take a side and defend it, even if it's a silly one.
cards: Cereal is a type of soup.
Phone calls are worse than going to the dentist.
Breakfast food is better at dinner time.
Sequels are usually better than the original film.
Sandwiches taste better when they're cut into triangles.
It's rude to send a voice message.
Weekends should be three days long.
Socks with sandals are a good idea.
Going to the gym is boring.

ind: Show the hot take. The student says agree or disagree on a 1–10 scale and why.
You take the opposite side, even if you agree, and argue back.
Ask them to find one argument for the other side.
pair: Partners each give a number from 1 (totally disagree) to 10 (totally agree).
The person with the lower number must convince the other to move at least two points.
Swap who starts on the next card.
grp: Show the hot take. Students stand on an imaginary line: one wall = agree, other wall = disagree.
Ask students at both ends to defend their position.
Anyone can move if they're convinced. Ask the people who moved why.

end: Which hot take divided the class the most?

name: Most Likely To…
desc: Who in the class is most likely to…? Nominate someone and explain why.
instr: Who in this class is most likely to do this? Choose a classmate (or yourself!) and explain why. Keep it kind!
ph: I think … is most likely to… because…
I'd say me, to be honest, because…
cards: get lost in their own city
arrive late to their own wedding

ind: Private student version: ask 'Who in your family / group of friends is most likely to…?' and let them explain.
Ask for a real story that proves it.
Answer one yourself.
pair: Pairs think of people they both know (classmates, famous people).
They agree on one name per card and give a reason.
Compare with another pair.
grp: Show the card. On 3, everyone points at a classmate.
The student with most fingers pointing at them asks two people why.
Keep it light: ban answers that could be hurtful.

end: Who got the most votes today? Do they agree?

name: Silly Conspiracies
desc: Convince the class of a completely absurd (and harmless) conspiracy theory.
instr: Your job is to convince everyone this is true. Invent 'evidence', use statistics and sound very serious.
ph: Think about it: why else would…?
cards: Cats invented the internet so we'd post photos of them.
The moon is made of cheese, and astronauts keep it secret.
Socks disappear because washing machines eat them.
Every time you sneeze, a cloud is born.
Dogs can read, but they pretend they can't.
Mondays were invented by coffee companies.
Your fridge light stays on when the door is closed.
Penguins can fly, but only when nobody is looking.

ind: Give the student two minutes to prepare three pieces of 'evidence'.
You play the sceptic and ask tricky questions.
Then swap: you defend one and they attack.
pair: Student A defends the theory for one minute; Student B is the sceptical journalist.
B must ask at least three questions starting 'But how do you explain…?'
Swap roles on the next card.
grp: Groups of three prepare the 'evidence' in three minutes.
One speaker per group presents. The class asks questions.
Vote: which group was the most convincing?

end: Which theory was so convincing you almost believed it?

name: The Pitch
desc: Dragons' Den style: pitch a ridiculous invention and get investors to say yes.
instr: You're on a TV show for inventors. Pitch this invention in one minute. The investors will ask questions and decide if they invest.
ph: Our product solves a problem everyone has:…
We're asking for… in exchange for…
cards: A fridge that locks itself at midnight
Shoes that tell you when you're lost
A pillow that records your dreams
A mug that keeps coffee hot for a week
An app that replies to messages for you
A sofa that makes you do exercise
A pen that corrects your spelling

ind: The student pitches; you're the investor and ask the three questions.
Decide: invest or not? Explain why.
Swap: you pitch the next one.
pair: Each pair pitches to another pair, who play investors.
Investors must ask at least three questions, then decide.
Swap roles.
grp: Teams prepare a pitch for 3 minutes.
3–4 students act as investors with an imaginary €100,000 to share.
Investors announce who gets their money and why.

end: Who got the most investment? Would you really buy it?

name: Rank It
desc: Put five things in order. Then agree on one ranking with your partner.
instr: Put these in order from best (1) to worst (5). Then compare with a partner and agree on one ranking.

ind: The student ranks the five and explains each position.
You give your ranking and disagree on at least two.
Agree on one ranking together.
pair: Each student ranks alone (30 seconds).
Pairs compare and must agree on one ranking in two minutes.
Pairs join another pair and agree again.
grp: Show the slide. Students rank individually.
Ask a few students for their number one and last. Count hands for each option.
Build a class ranking on the board.

end: Which ranking caused the biggest argument?

name: Questions Only
desc: Improvise a scene where you can only speak in questions.
instr: Act out the scene with your partner, but you can ONLY speak in questions. Hesitate, repeat or answer with a statement… and you're out!
ex: A: Excuse me, is this your dog? B: Why are you asking? A: Didn't you see it ate my sandwich? B: Are you sure it was my dog?
cards: Ordering in a very strange restaurant
A job interview for a superhero
Returning a broken phone to the shop
Two strangers stuck in a lift
A parent and a teenager at 3 am

ind: You and the student act the scene, questions only.
The first one to make a statement loses the round.
Do three quick rounds, then review question forms that came up.
pair: Pairs act the scene for one minute.
When someone makes a statement or hesitates, swap in a new partner (or restart).
Count how many questions each pair managed.
grp: Two volunteers act at the front.
When one makes a mistake, the class shouts 'Out!' and a new student replaces them.
Keep the same scene running as long as possible.

end: What was the funniest question of the day?

name: Slide Roulette
desc: PowerPoint karaoke: give an expert talk on a ridiculous topic you've never seen before.
instr: You are a world expert on this topic. Give a two-minute talk using the three points. You've never seen the slide before… improvise!
ph: Good morning, everyone. Today I'm going to talk about…

cards.t: The secret life of office chairs
Why cats are better managers than humans
Pizza as a form of art
Teaching your grandmother to use TikTok
The economics of a children's lemonade stand
Why we should all have a nap at work
The dangers of being too polite
A day in the life of a supermarket trolley

ind: The student sees the slide for the first time and talks for two minutes.
You ask two 'audience' questions at the end.
Swap roles on the next slide.
pair: Pairs take turns presenting to each other.
The listener asks one question at the end.
Give feedback on linkers used.
grp: Choose a volunteer (or use Pick a student). They see the slide for the first time with the class.
Start the timer: two minutes.
The audience asks two questions. Applause is mandatory!

end: Who was the most convincing expert today?

name: What Happens If…?
desc: Say what always happens in everyday situations, then compare with the answer.
instr: What always happens? Answer with a full sentence. Then add one more 'If…' fact about your own life.
ex: If you don't sleep, you feel tired. If I drink coffee after 6 pm, I can't sleep.

cards.t: If you don't water a plant…
If you mix red and blue…
If you leave milk out of the fridge…
If you don't charge your phone…
If you eat too much chocolate…
If you press the snooze button…
If you drop your phone in water…
If you don't wear sun cream at the beach…
If you shout in a library…
If you don't practise a language…

ind: Show the beginning. The student finishes it before you reveal the answer.
Ask: 'And in your case?' The student makes one personal zero-conditional sentence.
Correct the structure: present + present (no 'will').
pair: Partners take turns finishing the sentence before the reveal.
After each card, each partner says one personal 'If I…, I…' habit.
Find one habit you both share.
grp: Show the card. Students write their ending on a mini whiteboard or say it to a partner.
Reveal: who said the same?
Pick two students to share a personal 'If I…' habit.

end: Write three 'If…' facts about your daily routine.

name: Chain Reaction
desc: Build a chain of consequences: each result becomes the next 'If…'.
instr: Continue the chain. Take the result of the last sentence and start a new one with 'If…'. How long can you keep it going?
ex: If it rains tomorrow, I'll stay at home. If I stay at home, I'll watch films all day. If I watch films all day, I'll eat too much popcorn…
cards: If I win the match on Saturday,…
If I wake up late tomorrow,…
If I go to the party tonight,…
If I pass all my exams,…
If my best friend visits me,…
If I save some money this month,…
If the teacher gives us homework,…
If I miss the last bus tonight,…

ind: You and the student take turns adding one link to the chain.
Each link must start with the result of the previous one.
Stop at 8 links and read the whole chain back.
pair: Partners alternate links for one minute (use the timer).
Count the links. Can they beat their score on the next card?
Swap who starts.
grp: Students stand in a circle. Each adds one link.
Anyone who hesitates for more than 5 seconds or makes a mistake sits down.
Last students standing win.

end: What was the funniest chain? Where did it end?

name: What Would You Do?
desc: Real-life dilemmas: what would you do, and why?
instr: Read the situation. What would you do? Explain why, and say what you definitely wouldn't do.
ph: If I were in that situation, I'd…
If it were me, I might…
q: Would your answer change if nobody was watching?
cards: You see your friend's partner on a date with someone else.
A shop gives you too much change.
You win a free trip, but it's on your best friend's wedding day.
Your boss offers you a promotion in another city.
You break a glass at a friend's house and nobody sees it.
A stranger asks you to look after their dog for an hour.
You hear your neighbours arguing loudly at 2 am.
Someone in a restaurant is talking very loudly on the phone.
You get a message meant for someone else.
You're offered your dream job, but the salary is lower.
Your friend asks what you think of their terrible haircut.

ind: The student answers and explains. Push with 'And if…?' to change one detail.
Share what you would do and disagree on purpose.
Note errors with 'would' + infinitive and 'If I were…'.
pair: Each partner answers; the other asks 'What if…?' with a new detail.
They must find one thing they would both do.
Swap who starts.
grp: Show the dilemma and give 30 seconds to think.
Vote with hands for the two most popular options.
Ask one student from each side to justify their choice.

end: Which dilemma was the hardest? Did anyone change their mind?

name: Imagine If…
desc: Imagine a different world and describe how life would change.
instr: Imagine this was true. How would life be different? Think about school, work, free time and your own day.
cards: If we only needed to sleep one hour a day
If everybody spoke the same language
If it was summer all year
If cars were banned in cities

ind: The student gives at least three consequences.
Ask about their personal day: 'What would you do?'
Correct 'would' in the result clause and past simple in the if-clause.
pair: Partners take turns adding one consequence each, for one minute.
Then decide: would the world be better or worse?
Share the best idea with the class.
grp: Show the card. Groups list as many consequences as possible in 2 minutes.
Groups read their lists. Repeated ideas don't count.
The group with the most original ideas wins.

end: Which world would you like to live in?

name: Sliding Doors
desc: One small change in the past. How would everything have been different?
instr: Imagine this had happened differently. Build a chain: what would or wouldn't have happened?
ex: If I hadn't missed the bus, I wouldn't have met Ana. If I hadn't met Ana, I wouldn't have joined the choir…
cards: You missed the bus this morning.
The Titanic had seen the iceberg in time.
You had been born in another country.
The internet had never been invented.
You had chosen a different school or job.
You hadn't gone out last Saturday.
You had said yes to the last invitation you said no to.
Your favourite band had never formed.
You hadn't met your best friend.

ind: The student builds a chain of at least four third-conditional links.
Ask about real regrets: 'Is there anything you would have done differently?'
Drill the contraction: 'I'd have' / 'I wouldn't have'.
pair: Partners alternate links until they reach something surprising.
Then each shares one real past decision and how life could have been different.
Report the funniest chain to the class.
grp: Show the card. One student starts, the next continues the chain.
Write the chain on the board as it grows.
At the end, the class reads it aloud together.

end: Is there a small decision in your life that changed everything?

name: Mixed Up Lives
desc: A different past, a different present: talk about who you'd be now.
instr: Imagine this had been different in the past. How would your life be different NOW?
ph: If I had…, I would be… now.
If I hadn't…, I wouldn't have… now.
If I were…, I would have… (past)
ex: If I had studied medicine, I would be working in a hospital now. If I weren't so shy, I would have spoken to her yesterday.
cards: If you had been born 100 years ago…
If you had studied something completely different…
If you had grown up in another country…
If you had never learnt to use a computer…
If you had been born a twin…
If you had become famous as a child…
If you weren't afraid of anything… (what would you have done last year?)
If you were a morning person… (what would you have done this morning?)
If you had moved house five years ago…
If you had saved all the money you've spent on coffee…
If you spoke five languages… (what would you have done differently?)
If you had said yes to your first job offer…

ind: The student answers with at least two mixed-conditional sentences.
Ask them to switch: past→present, then present→past.
Highlight the two patterns on the board.
pair: Partners take turns. The listener checks the tenses and asks one follow-up.
After each card, partners compare: whose 'other life' sounds better?
Swap who starts.
grp: Show the card and give a minute of thinking time.
Pick students to share; the class identifies which pattern they used.
Finish with a quick correction round.

end: Write one mixed conditional about your own life.

name: Who Am I?
focus: Present simple for routines: I get up…, I work…, I don't…, I usually…
desc: Be a person, animal or object and describe your typical day. The others guess who you are.
instr: Only the speaker looks at the card. Describe your typical day as if you were that person, animal or thing. Don't say the word! The others guess.
ex: I sleep all day. At night I go out. I don't like garlic. I never look in mirrors… (a vampire)

ind: The student looks at the card and describes their day in five sentences; you guess.
Then swap: you describe, they guess.
Correct third-person -s when they ask 'Do you…? / Does it…?'
pair: Hide the slide: one partner looks, the other doesn't.
The listener can ask yes/no questions: 'Do you work at night?'
Swap after each guess.
grp: One student comes to the front and looks at the card (press Hide card for the class).
The class asks yes/no questions in the present simple.
Whoever guesses becomes the next speaker.

end: Which one was the hardest to guess?

name: Mime Time
focus: Present continuous for actions in progress: Are you …ing? You're …ing!
desc: Mime a funny action. The class guesses what you're doing right now.
instr: Only the actor looks at the card. Mime the action. The class must guess using the present continuous: 'Are you…ing?'
ph: Is it heavy? Are you enjoying it?
No, I'm not. Yes, I am!
cards: taking a selfie in the rain
eating spaghetti on a first date

ind: Take turns: you mime, the student guesses, then swap.
Insist on full questions: 'Are you…ing?' not just the verb.
Add a follow-up: 'Why are you doing that?'
pair: Partners take turns miming, using the hidden slide.
The guesser can only ask yes/no questions.
Count how many they guess in 3 minutes.
grp: Press Hide card. The actor comes to look and mimes for the class.
Teams take turns guessing with 'Are you…ing?'
A correct guess = 1 point; a correct guess with perfect grammar = 2.

end: Who was the best actor today?

name: The Evidence
focus: Present perfect continuous for visible results: You've been …ing! Have you been …ing?
desc: Look at the evidence and work out what someone has been doing.
instr: Look at the evidence. What has this person been doing? Make at least three guesses. The 'suspect' invents the true story.
cards: Your face is covered in paint.
You're out of breath and very sweaty.
Your eyes are red and you have tissues everywhere.
There's flour all over the kitchen.
Your hands are full of soil.
Your hair is wet but it isn't raining.
You're smiling and you can't stop.
There are 15 empty coffee cups on your desk.

ind: You're the 'suspect'. The student makes three guesses, then you invent the true story.
Swap roles on the next card.
Contrast with the present perfect simple: 'I've painted the kitchen' vs 'I've been painting'.
pair: Partner A is the suspect, Partner B makes three guesses.
The suspect reveals what they have really been doing, the more creative the better.
Swap.
grp: Choose a 'suspect' to stand at the front.
The class makes guesses: the most creative correct sentence wins a point.
The suspect tells the true story.

end: What have YOU been doing this week?

name: Have You Ever… (Liar Edition)
focus: Have you ever…? (present perfect) → When/where/what happened? (past simple)
desc: Answer 'yes' to every question, even if it's a lie. The others ask follow-ups to catch you.
instr: Ask 'Have you ever…?' The speaker ALWAYS says yes. Then ask three follow-up questions in the past simple. True or lie? Vote!
ph: Yes, I have. / No, I haven't.
When did you…? Where were you?
What happened next? Who was with you?
cards: fallen asleep in class or at work

ind: The student asks you; you answer yes and they ask three follow-ups. Then swap.
They decide: truth or lie?
Highlight the switch: Have you ever…? → When did you…?
pair: Partners take turns. The speaker secretly decides to tell the truth or lie.
The listener asks three past simple questions and guesses.
1 point for a correct guess, 1 point for a successful lie.
grp: One student in the hot seat. The class asks follow-ups (max five).
Everyone votes: truth or lie?
Reveal and choose the next student.

end: Who was the best liar? What was the most surprising true story?

name: Epic Weekend
focus: Past simple for a sequence of events: First I…, then I…, after that…
desc: Tell the story of your weekend, but it must include three surprising things.
instr: Tell the story of your last weekend. It must include the three things on the card! Make it believable. The others ask questions.
end: Whose weekend would you like to have had?

name: When It Happened
focus: Past continuous + past simple: I was …ing when…
desc: Something strange happened. What were you doing at that exact moment?
instr: Imagine this happened yesterday. What were you doing when it happened? What did you do next?
cards: The lights went out in the whole city.
A cow walked into the classroom.
Your phone rang with an unknown number at 3 am.
It started snowing in the middle of summer.
Someone famous knocked on your door.
You heard a very strange noise in the kitchen.
Your best friend sent you a message: 'Help!'
A bird flew into the room.
The internet stopped working all over the world.
You saw yourself on the TV news.

ind: The student answers with 'I was…ing when…' and continues the story.
Ask what other people were doing.
You answer too and compare.
pair: Each partner says what they were doing and what they did next.
Then they combine both stories into one.
Share the funniest with the class.
grp: Show the card. Go round the class: everyone says what they were doing (no repeats!).
Pick one answer and build a class story from it.
Highlight the two tenses on the board.

end: What were you doing yesterday at 8 pm?

name: The Backstory
focus: Past perfect for what happened before: She had already…, He hadn't…
desc: Something happened. Invent what had happened before to explain it.
instr: Explain the situation: what had happened before? Give at least three possible explanations, then choose the best one.
ph: By the time…, they had already…
cards: When Ana got home, she was absolutely furious.
Tom arrived at work in his pyjamas.
The teacher came into the class and started laughing.
When we arrived at the party, everybody had gone.
He opened the fridge and screamed.
She was crying at the airport, but she was smiling.
The dog was sitting on the sofa looking very guilty.
My neighbour knocked on my door at midnight holding a cake.
The whole team was singing in the office on Monday morning.
When I got to the cinema, I realised I was alone.
My grandmother suddenly bought a motorbike.
The chef walked out of his own restaurant.

ind: The student gives three explanations with the past perfect.
You choose the best one and ask questions about it.
Correct: 'had + past participle' for the earlier action.
pair: Partners compete: who can give the most original explanation?
Then they tell the full story in order.
Swap who starts.
grp: Show the situation. Groups have one minute to invent the backstory.
Each group tells theirs; the class votes for the best.
Write a perfect example on the board.

end: Which backstory would make the best film?

name: Back in My Day…
focus: used to / would for past habits: We used to…, We didn't use to…, We would…
desc: It's the year 2080 and you're very old. Tell the young people how life used to be in the 2020s.
instr: It's 2080 and you're a grandparent. Tell the 'kids' how things used to be when you were young. Then talk about your real childhood.
ph: Back in my day, we used to…
Can you believe we used to…?
ex: Back in my day, we used to carry our phones in our pockets! And we would wait 5 minutes for a pizza delivery. Terrible!
q: How did it use to be in YOUR childhood?

ind: The student plays the 2080 grandparent; you're the shocked grandchild.
Then talk about their real childhood: 'When I was a child, I used to…'
Note the difference between used to and would.
pair: One partner is the 2080 grandparent, the other asks questions.
Swap, then compare real childhoods.
Find three things you both used to do.
grp: Show the topic. Volunteers play the grandparent for one minute.
The class reacts and asks questions.
Finish with a real 'When I was a child…' round.

end: What do you think people in 2080 will find funny about us?

name: Fortune Teller
focus: will / going to / might for predictions: You will…, You're going to…, You might…
desc: Read your partner's future. Make the predictions as dramatic as possible!
instr: You're a fortune teller. Look into the crystal ball and predict your partner's future about this topic. Your partner reacts!
ph: I can see that you will…

ind: You're the fortune teller first, then the student.
Push for three predictions per topic.
Point out 'going to' when there's evidence: 'Look at the clouds! It's going to rain.'
pair: Partners take turns being the fortune teller.
The 'client' must react: 'Really? When will that happen?'
At the end, each says which prediction they hope comes true.
grp: Choose a fortune teller and a client to come to the front.
The class can add 'extra visions'.
Rotate every topic.

end: Which prediction do you hope will come true?

name: Sorry, I'll Be Busy
focus: Future continuous for actions in progress in the future: I'll be …ing at 6.
desc: Someone keeps inviting you to boring things. Invent creative reasons why you'll be busy.
instr: Your partner invites you to this. You don't want to go! Say what you'll be doing at that time. Be creative. Your partner suggests another time…
ph: Sorry, at that time I'll be…ing.
I'd love to, but I'll be…ing all day.
cards: Can you help me move house on Saturday at 9 am?
Do you want to come to my cousin's poetry reading tonight?
Can you look after my five cats this weekend?
Shall we go running at 6 am tomorrow?
Come to my 3-hour presentation about stamps!
Can you help me paint my fence on Sunday?
Do you want to watch all 8 Harry Potter films tomorrow?
Can you drive me to the airport at 4 am?
Want to help me clean the garage next Saturday?
Can you come to my karaoke practice tonight?

ind: You invite; the student refuses with 'I'll be…ing'. Keep suggesting new times.
Swap roles.
Contrast: 'I'll be working at 6' vs 'I'll work tomorrow'.
pair: Partner A invites and suggests three different times.
Partner B must refuse each time with a new excuse.
Swap after each card.
grp: One student invites the class; volunteers refuse with creative excuses.
The class votes for the most creative excuse.
Rotate the 'inviter'.

end: What will you be doing this time tomorrow?

name: By the Year 2050
focus: Future perfect: By 2050, we will have…; Future continuous: People will be …ing.
desc: Predict what will have changed by a certain point in the future.
instr: Make predictions. What will have happened by then? What will people be doing? Agree or disagree with each other.
ph: I don't think we'll have… by…
By the time I'm…, I'll have…
cards: By the end of this year, I…
By the end of this course, we…

ind: The student makes three predictions; you agree or disagree.
Do the personal cards (By the time I'm 40…) slowly and ask why.
Point out 'by' + future perfect.
pair: Partners make predictions and rate each other's: likely, possible or impossible.
Find one prediction you both agree on.
Share it with the class.
grp: Show the card. Groups write three predictions in two minutes.
Groups read them; the class votes for the most likely.
Write the best ones on the board as a 'time capsule'.

end: Write one prediction for yourself to read in 10 years.

name: Dear Agony Aunt
focus: Advice: You should…, You ought to…, You'd better…, If I were you, I'd…
desc: Give advice to people with funny or tricky problems.
instr: This person has written to the advice column. Give them at least three pieces of advice. What shouldn't they do?
cards: My flatmate eats all my food.
I've accidentally liked my ex's photo from 5 years ago.
My best friend sings terribly but wants to go on a talent show.
I can't stop checking my phone.
My boss always calls me on Sundays.
My dog hates my new partner.
I've said yes to two parties on the same night.
My neighbour practises the drums at midnight.
I want to learn English but I have no time.
I told everyone I can cook… and now I have to cook for 10 people.
My parents want to join my group chat.
I'm scared of flying but I've won a free trip to Japan.

ind: The student gives three pieces of advice; you choose the best and ask why.
Then the student writes you a problem.
Practise softening: 'Maybe you could…'
pair: Partner A reads the problem as if it's theirs; B gives advice.
A chooses the best advice.
Swap.
grp: Show the problem. Students have one minute to write their best advice.
Read a few aloud; the class votes.
Highlight should / ought to / had better on the board.

end: What's the best advice anyone has ever given you?

name: The Alien Rulebook
focus: Rules: You have to…, You must…, You mustn't…, You don't have to…, You can…
desc: An alien is coming to live in your town. Teach it the rules nobody explains.
instr: An alien has just arrived and wants to fit in. Explain the rules for this place: what you have to do, what you mustn't do and what you don't have to do.

ind: The student explains the rules; you're the confused alien and ask 'Why?'
Ask for one rule that's different in another country.
Contrast mustn't vs don't have to.
pair: One partner is the alien and asks questions; the other explains.
Swap every card.
Find a rule that you think is silly.
grp: Show the place. The class gives rules; you write them in three columns (have to / mustn't / don't have to).
Ask: which rule is the most important?
Vote on the silliest rule.

end: Which rule would the alien find the strangest?

name: Whose Bag Is This?
focus: Deduction: It must be…, It might/could be…, It can't be…
desc: Look at what's inside a lost bag and work out who it belongs to.
instr: This bag was found on a train. Look at what's inside. Who does it belong to? What do they do? Use must, might and can't.
ph: It might be… / It could be…

ind: The student makes at least three deductions; you challenge them ('Are you sure?').
Ask them to describe the owner's day.
Contrast must / might / can't with how sure they are.
pair: Partners make deductions and agree on one 'owner profile'.
Compare with another pair.
Swap who starts.
grp: Show the bag. Groups write a profile of the owner in two minutes.
Groups present; the class decides which is most logical.
Write the best deductions on the board.

end: What would someone deduce about you from YOUR bag?

name: What Must Have Happened?
focus: Past deduction: must have / might have / can't have + past participle; criticism: should have…
desc: Mysterious situations: work out what happened and who should have done things differently.
instr: What must have happened? Give three possible explanations, then say what someone should or shouldn't have done.
cards: The kitchen is flooded and the dog is wet.
Your friend didn't come to your birthday party.
The car has a parking ticket and a broken mirror.
Your phone has 47 missed calls from your mum.
The cake in the fridge has a big bite out of it.
Your neighbour's garden is full of footprints.
The teacher came to class with one shoe.
All the lights in the office were on on Monday morning.
Your plant is dead after your holiday.
There's a stranger asleep on your sofa.
The pizza arrived two hours late and cold.

ind: The student gives three deductions, then one criticism.
Ask them to tell the 'true story' in the end.
Contrast must have (sure) vs might have (possible).
pair: Partners take turns making deductions until one sounds right.
Then they decide who should have done what.
Share with the class.
grp: Show the situation. Groups think of the most logical and the funniest explanation.
Groups present; vote for each.
Correct past participles on the board.

end: Tell us about something you should have done differently this week.

name: Corrupt a Wish
focus: I wish I had/could…, If only…, I wish I hadn't… — and the genie's twist: 'Granted, but…'
desc: Make a wish. The next person grants it… but adds a terrible twist.
instr: Make a wish about the topic: 'I wish I…'. The next student is the genie: 'Granted, but…' and adds a twist. Then they make a new wish.
ph: I wish I had / could / were…
Now I wish I hadn't wished for that!
ex: A: I wish I could fly. B: Granted, but you can only fly at 2 km per hour. B: I wish I were rich. C: Granted, but all your money is in coins.

ind: You're the genie first. The student wishes, you twist it. Then swap.
Finish with a real regret: 'I wish I hadn't…'
Point out: wish + past simple (present), wish + past perfect (past).
pair: Partners take turns wishing and twisting for 2 minutes per topic.
Count the twists: the funniest pair shares one.
Swap topics.
grp: Students sit in a circle. The wish travels round the class.
Anyone who can't think of a twist in 5 seconds is out.
Vote for the cruellest twist.

end: What's one thing you really wish you could change about your week?

name: It Wasn't Me!
focus: Passive to avoid blame: The vase was broken…, The cake has been eaten…, It must have been…
desc: Something went wrong and you don't want to be blamed. Explain it with the passive.
instr: Your parent, boss or flatmate is angry. Explain what happened without saying it was you! Use the passive.
ph: It must have been… by the cat
cards: All the biscuits have been eaten.
The walls have been painted pink.
The wifi password has been changed.
The dog has been dyed blue.
The fridge door was left open all night.

ind: You're the angry parent or boss and ask questions; the student defends themselves with the passive.
Swap roles.
Show how the passive hides who did it.
pair: One partner accuses, the other avoids the blame.
The accuser decides: guilty or not guilty?
Swap.
grp: Groups play a family. 'Parents' ask questions; 'siblings' blame each other using the passive.
Act out the best one for the class.
Write the best passive excuses on the board.

end: What's the best excuse you've ever heard?

name: Made, Built, Written…
revealTag: Passive quiz · say the full sentence
focus: Past passive with by: It was painted by…, It was invented by…
desc: A passive quiz: who made it? Say the full sentence before the answer is revealed.
instr: Who made it? Answer with a full passive sentence: 'It was painted by…'. Then tell your partner one more fact you know.
ph: I think it was built in…

cards.ans: It was painted by Leonardo da Vinci.
It was designed by Antoni Gaudí.
It was written by J.K. Rowling.
It was discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928.
It was invented by Tim Berners-Lee in 1989.
It was painted by Pablo Picasso in 1937.
It was written by William Shakespeare.
It was discovered by Marie and Pierre Curie in 1898.
It was developed by Albert Einstein.
It was written by Miguel de Cervantes.

ind: The student answers in a full passive sentence before you reveal.
Ask: 'Where was it made? When?' to get more passives.
Then ask them to make a quiz question for you.
pair: Pairs answer before each reveal; one point per correct full sentence.
After the quiz, each pair writes two new questions for another pair.
Swap questions.
grp: Teams answer on mini whiteboards: only full passive sentences score.
Reveal and give points.
Teams invent a question for the other team.

end: Make a passive question about your city for a partner.

name: The Lazy Millionaire
focus: Causative: I have my… done, I get someone to…, I had it repaired
desc: You're a millionaire who never does anything yourself. Explain how you get things done.
instr: You're a very lazy millionaire. Explain how you get this done — you never do it yourself! Then say what you really do yourself in real life.

ind: The student plays the millionaire; you're the journalist asking questions.
Switch to real life: 'When did you last have your hair cut?'
Compare 'I cut my hair' vs 'I had my hair cut'.
pair: One partner is the millionaire, the other the interviewer.
Swap, then compare what you do yourselves in real life.
Who's the laziest?
grp: Show the card. Volunteers answer as millionaires.
Then a real-life round: hands up if you do it yourself.
Write a few causative sentences on the board.

end: What would you pay someone to do for you if you could?

name: Pardon? What Did She Say?
focus: Reported speech: She said (that)…, He told me…, She asked if…, He wanted to know…
desc: Grandma can't hear well. Repeat what people said using reported speech.
instr: Student A says the sentence. Student B is grandma and says 'Pardon?' Student C reports it: 'She said that…'. Watch the tenses!
cards: "I've never been so tired in my life."

ind: You say the sentence, play grandma, and the student reports it. Then swap.
Show the backshift: am → was, will → would, have → had.
Add a twist: report what someone said to them this week.
pair: Groups of three: speaker, grandma, reporter. Rotate roles every card.
Grandma can say 'Pardon?' twice: the reporter must say it in a different way the second time.
Report the funniest sentence to the class.
grp: Choose a speaker and a grandma. The class reports in turns.
Points for correct tense changes.
Finish with a gossip round: 'I heard that…'

end: Report one thing someone said to you this week.

name: The Never-Ending Sentence
focus: Relative clauses: who, which, that, where, whose, when
desc: Build one huge sentence together, adding relative clauses one by one.
instr: Continue the sentence by adding a relative clause (who, which, that, where, whose, when). How long can the class make it?
ex: This is the man who lives in the house which has a garden where a dog whose name is Max sleeps…
cards: There's a shop in my town…

ind: You and the student take turns adding a clause until it breaks.
Then say the whole sentence from the beginning.
Focus on whose and where.
pair: Partners alternate clauses for two minutes.
Count the clauses. Try to beat your record on the next card.
Read the final sentence to the class.
grp: Go round the class: each student repeats the sentence and adds a clause.
If someone forgets, the sentence starts again.
Write the record sentence on the board.

end: What's the longest sentence we built?

name: The Most… Ever
focus: Superlative + present perfect: the best… I've ever…; comparatives to compare answers
desc: Talk about the best, worst and strangest things you've ever experienced.
instr: Answer with a superlative and the present perfect, then tell the story. Your partner compares: 'Mine was even worse than yours!'
ph: It was the most… I've ever…
cards: the best present you've ever received
the worst meal you've ever eaten
the most beautiful place you've ever visited
the strangest dream you've ever had
the most embarrassing moment you've ever had
the longest journey you've ever made
the best concert you've ever been to
the most boring film you've ever seen
the scariest thing you've ever done
the funniest person you've ever met
the most expensive thing you've ever bought
the hardest exam you've ever taken

ind: The student answers and tells the story; you compare with yours.
Push for comparatives: 'Was it worse than…?'
Correct 'the most + adjective' and 'I've ever'.
pair: Partners answer and compare: whose was the best/worst?
Each pair chooses one story to tell the class.
Swap who starts.
grp: Show the card. Students answer in small groups.
Each group picks the 'winner' and tells the class.
Vote for the most extreme story.

end: What's the best thing that has happened to you this week?

name: Can't Stand, Can't Live Without
focus: Verb patterns: love/enjoy/can't stand/don't mind + -ing; want/hope/would like/decide + to
desc: Say how you feel about everyday activities and find classmates with the same tastes.
instr: How do you feel about this? Use a verb + -ing or + to. Then try to convince your partner to like it as much as you do (or hate it!).
ph: I'd like to / I'm hoping to…

ind: The student gives their opinion with two different verb patterns.
Ask: 'Would you like to… more often?' to get the infinitive.
Share yours and disagree.
pair: Partners find out who likes each activity more.
Each tries to convince the other in 30 seconds.
Find two things you both can't stand.
grp: Show the card. Students move: love it (left), don't mind (middle), can't stand (right).
Ask people in each group to explain.
Keep a class 'top 3 most hated' list.

end: What's something you'd like to start doing?

name: Here's the Answer
focus: Question forms in all tenses: word order, auxiliaries (do/did/have/will), subject questions
desc: Jeopardy style: you get the answer, you invent the question.
instr: Here's the answer. What was the question? Think of at least two different questions. Then ask your partner one of them for real.
cards: In a small village near the sea.

ind: The student makes two questions for each answer.
Then ask them one of their questions for real.
Check auxiliaries and word order.
pair: Partners race: who can make the most correct questions in one minute?
Then they ask each other one question for real.
Swap who starts.
grp: Teams write as many questions as they can in one minute.
One point per correct question; two for a question nobody else has.
Ask some of the questions for real.

end: What's the most interesting question you heard today?

name: Drama Queen
focus: Negative inversion: Never have I…, Not only did…, Hardly had… when…, Under no circumstances…
desc: Turn boring sentences into dramatic ones with inversion, then tell a dramatic story.
instr: Say this sentence in the most dramatic way, starting with the word in brackets. Then continue the story with one more dramatic sentence!

cards.t: I have never seen such a mess. (Never…)
cards.ans: Never have I seen such a mess!

cards.t: She was late and she forgot the present. (Not only…)
cards.ans: Not only was she late, but she also forgot the present.

cards.t: We had just sat down when the fire alarm rang. (Hardly…)
cards.ans: Hardly had we sat down when the fire alarm rang.

cards.t: You must not open this door. (Under no circumstances…)
cards.ans: Under no circumstances must you open this door.

cards.t: I realised the truth only later. (Only later…)
cards.ans: Only later did I realise the truth.

cards.t: I have rarely eaten such a good meal. (Rarely…)
cards.ans: Rarely have I eaten such a good meal.

cards.t: He didn't say a word all evening. (Not once…)
cards.ans: Not once did he say a word all evening.

cards.t: You'll understand when you have children. (Only when…)
cards.ans: Only when you have children will you understand.

cards.t: I had no idea he was a spy. (Little…)
cards.ans: Little did I know that he was a spy.

cards.t: We arrived and it started to rain immediately. (No sooner…)
cards.ans: No sooner had we arrived than it started to rain.

ind: The student says the dramatic version before the reveal, with lots of drama.
Then continue the story with one more inverted sentence.
Focus on the auxiliary after the adverbial.
pair: Partners take turns: one reads, the other 'dramatises'.
After each reveal, they add one more line to the story.
Act out the best story.
grp: Show the sentence. Volunteers perform it like an actor.
The class checks the grammar on the reveal.
Groups write a mini-drama with three inversions and perform it.

end: Tell us about something that happened this week, as dramatically as you can.

name: What I Really Mean Is…
focus: Cleft sentences for emphasis: What I love about… is…, The thing that annoys me is…, It was… that…
desc: Give strong opinions with emphasis using cleft sentences.
instr: Say what you love and what annoys you about this topic. Start your sentences with 'What I…' or 'The thing that…'.
ph: The thing that drives me crazy is…
What I don't understand is why…

ind: The student gives one positive and one negative cleft sentence per topic.
Ask 'Why?' and get a second cleft sentence.
Compare: 'I love…' vs 'What I love is…' — which sounds stronger?
pair: Partners take turns. The listener must react with a cleft sentence too: 'What surprises me is…'
Swap every card.
Share the strongest opinion with the class.
grp: Show the topic. Go round the class: each student adds a cleft sentence without repeating.
Write the best ones on the board.
Vote for the most passionate opinion.

end: What I've learnt today is…

name: Linker Challenge
focus: Linkers and discourse markers: however, on the other hand, what's more, having said that, as a result…
desc: Talk for one minute about a topic and use all three linkers on the card.
instr: Talk for one minute about the topic. You MUST use all three linkers on the card. The others tick them off when they hear them!

ind: The student talks for one minute; you tick the linkers.
Give feedback: was each linker used correctly?
Repeat with a new card and a higher target.
pair: Partner A talks, B ticks the linkers and gives a point for each correct one.
Swap every card.
Who got the most points?
grp: Use Pick a student. The class listens and raises a hand at each linker.
Correct use = 1 point, wrong use = 0.
Finish with the three most useful linkers of the day.

end: Which linker will you use in your next writing?

name: Guess the Job
imgP: an invented person (not a real or famous person), face clearly visible, waist-up portrait in their workplace, with visual clues about their job ({x}) — do NOT show any text or name badge
focus: Speculation with a reason: He must be… because…, She might/could be…, He can't be… because…, She looks like… (clothes, place, objects, expression, posture…)
desc: Look at the photo and speculate about the person's job using must, might and can't.
instr: Look at the person in the photo. What's their job? Give at least two reasons: think about the place, the objects, their clothes, their expression or what they're doing.
ph: She might be a… / She could be a…
q: What else can you guess: age, personality, where they live?

cards.t: a man in a dark suit and tie speaking at a podium with several microphones and flags behind him
a very stylish young woman posing in front of a white backdrop with studio lights
a woman in a white coat with a stethoscope walking along a hospital corridor
a man with flour on his apron at 5 am, holding a tray of fresh bread
a woman in a hard hat and high-visibility vest looking at plans on a building site
a young man in paint-stained clothes holding brushes in front of a large canvas
a woman in a dark uniform with a cap and gold stripes on her sleeves, pulling a small suitcase at an airport
a man in a hoodie with headphones around his neck, sitting in front of three screens full of code
an older man with muddy boots and gloves pushing a wheelbarrow full of plants
a woman in a tracksuit with a whistle and a clipboard on a football pitch
a serious man in black clothes and sunglasses with an earpiece, standing outside a concert venue
a woman holding a microphone in front of a TV camera in the rain

ind: Show the photo. The student makes three speculations with reasons before you reveal.
Ask 'What else?': age, personality, a typical day.
Challenge them: 'Are you sure? Couldn't he be…?'
pair: Partners take turns speculating; the other must agree or disagree with a reason.
Before the reveal, they agree on one final answer.
One point for each correct guess.
grp: Show the photo. Teams have 30 seconds to agree on a job and two reasons.
Each team says its answer with a modal; then reveal.
Points for the correct job and for the best reasoning.

end: Who in this class looks like they could be a spy? Why?

name: Look and Say: Animals
imgP: a clear photo of {x}
q: What colour is it? Is it big or small? What sound does it make?
desc: Picture cards for little learners: name the animal, its colour and its sound.
instr: Look at the picture. What's this? Say the animal, then its colour and the sound it makes!

ind: Show the picture and ask 'What's this?'. Model the answer if needed.
Ask one more question: colour, size or sound. Act it out together.
Reveal the word and say it together, clapping the syllables.
pair: Pairs point at the screen and take turns asking 'What's this?'.
Add a mime: one child acts the animal, the other guesses.
grp: Show the picture. The whole class shouts the answer, then makes the sound.
Choose one child to act it out; the others copy.
Play 'Stand up if it's big!'

end: Which animal do you like best?

name: Look and Say: Food
imgP: a clear photo of {x}
q: Do you like it? Yummy or yucky?
desc: Picture cards: name the food and say if you like it.
instr: What's this? Do you like it? Rub your tummy for 'yummy' or make a face for 'yucky'!

ind: Show the picture, ask 'What's this?' and 'Do you like it?'.
Model 'I like… / I don't like…' with big gestures.
Reveal and repeat together.
pair: Children ask each other 'Do you like…?' and answer with a gesture.
grp: Show the picture. Children answer with 'Yummy!' or 'Yucky!' and a gesture.
Count hands: who likes it?
Make a class 'favourite food' list.

end: What's your favourite food?

name: Lost and Found
focus: Describing objects: It's big/small, It's made of…, It has…, It's the one with…
desc: You've lost something. Describe it so well that the others can 'find' it.
instr: Only the 'owner' looks at the card. You've lost this object! Describe it: colour, size, what it's made of, what's on it. The others guess what it is.
cards: a red water bottle with stickers
a blue backpack with a broken zip
a pencil case shaped like a cat
a black umbrella with white spots
a green jumper with a big star
a teddy bear with one ear
a pair of glasses in a purple case
a lunchbox with dinosaurs on it
a pink hat with a pompom

ind: The student describes; you guess. Then swap.
Push for 3 details: colour, size, material.
Ask 'Where did you lose it?'
pair: Hide the card for the guesser. The owner describes; the partner asks yes/no questions.
Swap.
grp: One child looks at the card (press H). The class asks questions: 'Is it big? Is it blue?'
Whoever guesses becomes the next owner.

end: Have you ever lost something important?

name: Pizza Party
focus: Suggesting and agreeing: Let's order…, We should…, What about…?, He can't eat…
desc: Plan a pizza order for the class with only three pizzas. Everyone has different needs!
instr: You can only order three pizzas for the whole group. Look at the problem on the card and agree which pizzas to order.
ph: We can't get… because… is allergic
cards: Two people are vegetarian and one person hates cheese.
Half the group loves spicy food, half hates it.
One person only eats pizza with pineapple.
Someone doesn't eat meat or fish.
The teacher wants a pizza too, with anchovies!
It's someone's birthday: they choose one pizza.
Nobody likes mushrooms except one person.

ind: Plan together: you play a difficult classmate with lots of demands.
The student must find a solution and explain it.
pair: Pairs agree on three pizzas in two minutes, then compare with another pair.
grp: Groups of four plan the order, then present it.
The class votes for the fairest plan.

end: What's the best pizza in the world?

name: Plan a Celebrity's Holiday
focus: Planning: They're going to…, They should…, They'll love… because…
desc: You're a travel agent for a very demanding (invented) celebrity. Plan their perfect week.
instr: You work for a travel agency. Plan a one-week holiday for this client: where, where to stay, what to do and what to avoid.
cards: A rock star who hates the sun and loves the night
A famous chef who wants to discover new food
A football player with an injured leg
A shy actor who doesn't want to be recognised
An influencer who needs 100 photos a day
A singer who's scared of planes
A billionaire who has been everywhere
A grandmother who has just won the lottery
A YouTuber who wants extreme adventures
A writer who needs total silence

ind: Plan the trip together; you're the difficult client and keep changing your mind.
pair: Pairs plan the week, then 'sell' it to another pair, who play the client.
grp: Groups plan a trip each, then present it like a TV ad.
The class votes for the trip they'd most like to go on.

end: Which client would be the worst to work for?

name: The Perfect Match
focus: Comparing and justifying: … would get on better with… because…, They're more… than…
desc: Read the profiles and decide who should share a flat, a holiday or a team.
instr: Read the four profiles. Make two pairs that would get on well. Explain your choice and say which pair would be a disaster!
ph: … and … would get on well because…

sub: Ana: tidy, early riser, hates noise
Ben: plays drums, night owl, cooks well
Dev: works from home, loves silence
Eli: loves museums and early mornings
Hana: needs a detailed plan for every day
Lola: talks a lot, great presenter
Max: only listens to heavy metal
Omar: loves stopping everywhere for photos
Pia: wants to arrive as fast as possible
Vic: wants to chat, not train
Xia: complete beginner, a bit shy

ind: The student pairs them up and justifies; you disagree with one pair.
pair: Pairs make their choice, then compare with another pair and negotiate a final answer.
grp: Groups decide, then defend their pairs to the class.

end: Who would be YOUR perfect flatmate?

name: The Museum Robbery
focus: Alibis and deduction: I was …ing, He must have…, She can't have… because…
desc: A painting was stolen last night. Read one clue per slide and work out who did it.
instr: Last night at 9 pm the famous painting 'Blue Moon' was stolen from the City Museum. There are four suspects. Read the clues one by one and decide who did it.
ph: She can't have done it because…
cards: The suspects: the guard (Mr Grey), the cleaner (Ms Rose), the director (Dr Black) and a visitor (Mr Green).
Clue 1: Mr Grey says he was watching football in the guard room.
Clue 2: The football match on TV was cancelled last night because of rain.
Clue 3: Ms Rose says she was cleaning the café on the ground floor.
Clue 4: The painting was on the second floor. The lift was broken.
Clue 5: Dr Black was having dinner at a restaurant. The waiter remembers her.
Clue 6: Mr Green left the museum at 8 pm. The camera at the door shows it.
Clue 7: There was a pair of wet shoes in the guard room.
Clue 8: Ms Rose's mop and bucket were found on the second floor.
Clue 9: Mr Grey has just bought a very expensive car.
Who stole the painting? Decide as a group and explain why. (Teacher: there's no single answer — the best argued solution wins!)

ind: Read the clues together. After each one, the student says who it could or couldn't be.
At the end they accuse someone and justify it.
pair: Pairs discuss each clue for one minute and keep a list of suspects.
At the end, pairs compare their solution with another pair.
grp: Groups of three or four are detective teams. Show one clue at a time.
At the end, each team accuses someone and gives three reasons.
The best-argued case wins.

end: Who did it? Was it the best-argued case or the truth?

name: The Class Playlist
focus: Opinions and preferences: I'd rather…, I can't stand…, It's more… than…, Let's include…
desc: Agree on a five-song playlist for a specific situation.
instr: Make a playlist of five songs for this situation. Everyone must agree! Explain why each song fits.
cards: A long bus trip on a school excursion
A party at the end of the year
A road trip with your family (everyone must like it!)

ind: The student chooses five songs and explains; you challenge two choices.
pair: Pairs negotiate a list of five songs, then present them.
grp: Groups agree on a playlist in five minutes. They can only keep a song if everyone accepts it.
Groups present and the class votes.

end: Which song would you never put on a playlist?

name: Disaster Plan
focus: Planning under pressure: We have to…, If we…, we'll…, We'd better…
desc: An emergency is coming. Agree on a plan in three minutes.
instr: You have three minutes to agree on a plan for this emergency. What will you do first? What will you take? Where will you go?
cards: A huge storm is arriving in two hours.
You're lost in the mountains and it's getting dark.
The power has gone off in the whole city for three days.
You're stuck in a lift with three strangers.
Your plane has landed on a desert island.
The school is snowed in. Nobody can leave until tomorrow.
Your car breaks down in the desert.
There's a zombie outbreak in your town.

ind: Start the 3-minute timer. You and the student agree on a five-step plan.
pair: Pairs make a plan, then compare it with another pair: whose would survive?
grp: Groups make a plan in three minutes and present it.
You (the teacher) add a new problem: they must adapt the plan.

end: Which plan would really work?
